pr_body:
- Use reference counting so nested `CacheStoreDatabase.use` share the same underlying database (rather than rereading it every time).
- Only write out the cache database file when it has changed.
- Cleanup cache database entries on formula or full `brew cleanup`.

Fixes #8690

pr_comments:
With this branch, performance of `brew install` improved to about 45 seconds total; we shaved off 1/3 of the total time. `brew cleanup` shrunk the linkage cache to under 500KB, so that's looking like a good longterm solution here. Notably, that's significantly larger than the size I'd get from deleting the linkage cache entirely and letting it be recreated, but at this size we're spending at most a second in the linkage checker - much more reasonable.

I do notice that the performance at this stage is still moderately worse than having no cache at all - I wonder if we've got more gains to be made. It could also be that the way we're handling this means that we have performance gains from caching with small numbers of formulae installed, but at certain cache sizes performance ends up actually being better without a cache.
Thank you @MikeMcQuaid. That performance gain is immensely helpful!

Thanks for testing @mistydemeo!

> I do notice that the performance at this stage is still moderately worse than having no cache at all - I wonder if we've got more gains to be made. It could also be that the way we're handling this means that we have performance gains from caching with small numbers of formulae installed, but at certain cache sizes performance ends up actually being better without a cache.

Yeh, there's definitely improvement to be had here although it's likely very dependent on your disk IO (doing this on an spinning platter HDD will take a lot longer to be slower, from previous measurements). The reference counting I've added here should mean you can wrap multiple calls to e.g. `undeclared_runtime_dependencies` with a top-level `CacheStoreDatabase.use(:linkage)` which should avoid reading the file from disk multiple times when not necessary.

issue_context.title: Linkage cache can grow to gargantuan sizes, causing poor post-install linkage checker performance
issue_context.body:
# Bug report - [x] ran `brew update` and can still reproduce the problem? - [x] ran `brew doctor`, fixed all issues and can still reproduce the problem? - [x] ran `brew config` and `brew doctor` and included their output with your issue? ## What you were trying to do (and why) When running `brew install`, I've noticed for awhile that Homebrew appears to hang after the install itself completes. I eventually figured out that it does complete, but it can take upwards of 60 seconds to complete even when the actual installation itself completes in under a second. After discussing it with @claui, it looks like I'm not the only person experiencing this. The factor I identified that's the same between both of us is that our linkage cache has grown to absolutely gargantuan proportions. Mine was 10MB of JSON, and hers was 20MB. At this point I'm quite positive that the linkage cache is the culprit, because deleting my cache and allowing it to be recreated results in a 30KB cache and `brew install` operations now complete instantaneously. I ran `brew prof --stackprof install blah`, and as expected it looks like most of the time is being spent in `CacheStoreDatabase`-related tasks. In particular it looks like `Formula#undeclared_runtime_dependencies` is slow when the cache gets this large, and it ended up being called 73 times here. This gets called several frames down from `check_broken_dependents`, via `Formula#runtime_installed_formula_dependents`. It feels more than a little ironic that caching can end up making things many times slower than not caching at all! If we're never cleaning this cache file, or not correctly cleaning it, it would explain how it managers to get so bloated over time. Here's the profiling data: https://gist.github.com/mistydemeo/638f2390bc3c4597fd3cc386e2b64900 ## What happened (include command output) The actual install process looks pretty much like normal; the user simply experiences a hang after the `installed` step, without any feedback that anything is happening.
